sections.b: After her fast, Esther goes in to the king unbidden and wins his favor (Esther 5:1–2). She does not ask at once but invites the king and Haman to two feasts, and at the second she reveals that she belongs to the people Haman has sold to be destroyed: "my life is what I ask... My people are what I want" (Esther 7:3). She names Haman as "the adversary, the enemy" and leaves the king's own part unspoken (Esther 7:6). When Haman is dead but his decree still stands, she pleads again in tears for "my people" and "my kin" (Esther 8:3–6). She asks for a second day of fighting in Susa (Esther 9:13), and finally writes "with all her authority" to make Purim binding (Esther 9:29–32), the only woman in the Hebrew Bible to issue a binding religious ruling for all Israel.

Esther's request that the Jews of Susa be allowed to fight on the 14th as well (Esther 9:13) has been judged in three ways: as vindictive (Paton and other older critics), as prudent because enemies remained in the capital (Baldwin, Jobes, Bush), and as a scene that explains why Susa and walled cities keep Purim on the 15th (Clines, Fox). The text gives no motive.

common: Esther is admired as a model of courage who risked her life for her people.
uncommon: Some readers think Esther's tact before the king (sparing him any blame) was as important to the rescue as her courage.

sections.h: From the king's gate to second in the empire (Esther 6–10)
sections.b: On the king's sleepless night, the records show that Mordecai once saved the king's life and was never rewarded (Esther 6:1–3). Haman, who came to ask for his death, must instead parade him through Susa in the king's clothes on the king's horse (Esther 6:10–11), a scene modeled on Joseph's honor in Egypt (Genesis 41:42–43). Mordecai receives Haman's signet ring and house (Esther 8:2), writes the counter-decree (Esther 8:9–14), walks out in royal clothes while the city cheers (Esther 8:15), and "kept on growing greater" (Esther 9:4), the words used of David (2 Samuel 5:10). He writes the letters that found Purim (Esther 9:20–28), and the book ends with him "next in rank after King Ahasuerus," working for his people's good (Esther 10:3).
sections.refs: Esther 6:1–11; Esther 8:2; Esther 8:9–15; Esther 9:4; Esther 9:20–28; Esther 10:3; Genesis 41:42–43; 2 Samuel 5:10

common: Mordecai is seen as the faithful Jew at a foreign court, like Joseph and Daniel.
uncommon: The Talmud notes he was accepted by the majority of his brothers, not all, and says some sages disapproved of his leaving Torah study for office (Bavli Megillah 16b).

sections.b: Haman leaves Esther's first feast happy, but Mordecai's refusal to rise spoils all his wealth and honor (Esther 5:9–13). On Zeresh's advice he builds a pole fifty cubits high for Mordecai (Esther 5:14). The next morning he must parade Mordecai through Susa (Esther 6:6–11), and his own household foretells his fall (Esther 6:13). At the second feast Esther names him, the king accuses him of assaulting the queen, and he is hanged on the pole he built (Esther 7:6–10), an example of the biblical theme that the plotter falls into his own pit (Psalm 7:15–16; Proverbs 26:27). His house goes to Esther, his ring to Mordecai (Esther 8:1–2), and his ten sons are killed and their bodies hung on the same pole (Esther 9:7–14). Mordecai's letter sums it up: his evil plot came back "on his own head" (Esther 9:25).
sections.refs: Esther 5:9–14; Esther 6:6–13; Esther 7:6–10; Esther 8:1–2; Esther 9:7–14; Esther 9:24–25; Psalm 7:15–16; Proverbs 26:27

common: Haman is the model of pride that comes before a fall.
uncommon: The Greek Esther calls Haman a Macedonian plotting to hand Persia to the Greeks (Addition E, and the Septuagint of 9:24).

sections.b: After the fighting of the 13th of Adar, the Jews of the provinces rest on the 14th and those of Susa on the 15th, and each makes its day one of feasting and joy (Esther 9:17–19). Mordecai's letters bind all Jews to keep both days every year, "sending portions of food to one another and presents to the needy" (Esther 9:22), and the days are named Purim after Haman's lot (Esther 9:24–26). The Jews take the feast on themselves, their descendants and "everyone who would join them" (Esther 9:27), and Esther's second letter confirms it (Esther 9:29–32). The Mishnah later fixed the 15th for cities walled since Joshua's day (Mishnah Megillah 1:1).

sections.h: Purim's origins: the book and the critics
sections.b: The book says Purim began with the rescue from Haman. Zimmern (1891) traced Purim to the Babylonian New Year, and Jensen (1892) read the story as a Jewish form of a Babylonian and Elamite myth (Mordecai = Marduk, Esther = Ishtar). Lagarde (1887) had proposed the Persian feast of the dead, Farvardigan, and Gaster (1950) argued that Purim adapted the Persian New Year. The name links are real, but no matching myth is known, and most scholars now see Purim as a feast of the eastern diaspora whose founding story is Esther, whatever older customs it absorbed. The earliest outside witness is "Mordecai's day" in 2 Maccabees 15:36.

common: Purim is kept with the Megillah reading, a feast, gifts of food to friends and gifts to the poor.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Purim regulations of Esther 9:20–32 were added to an older story that once ended at 8:17.

sections.h: Amalek's heirs defeated, and the plunder refused (Esther 9)
sections.b: Three times the Jews "kept their hands off the plunder" (Esther 9:10, 15, 16), though the decree allowed it (Esther 8:11). Many readers see a reversal of 1 Samuel 15, where Saul son of Kish and the people "took pity on Agag, and on the pick of the sheep and cattle" (1 Samuel 15:9) and Samuel asked, "Why did you swoop down on the spoil and do what is evil in the LORD's eyes?" (1 Samuel 15:19). Mordecai, of the family of Kish, and his people kill the heirs of Haman "the Agagite" and take nothing. Their "rest from their enemies" (Esther 9:16) recalls Deuteronomy's command: when God gives "rest from all your enemies," Israel is to wipe out the memory of Amalek (Deuteronomy 25:19). The Sabbath before Purim is Shabbat Zakhor, when Deuteronomy 25:17–19 is read.
sections.refs: Esther 9:10; Esther 9:15–16; Esther 8:11; 1 Samuel 15:9; 1 Samuel 15:19; Deuteronomy 25:17–19; Exodus 17:14

sections.b: The book's turning point is a king who cannot sleep, a record read at the right page, and an enemy who arrives too early (Esther 6:1–4). The Hebrew names no cause; the Greek says "the Lord took the sleep away from the king," and the Talmud reads "the king" as the King of the universe (Bavli Megillah 15b). From that night every plot of Haman's turns back on him, until "it was turned upside down" (Esther 9:1). Jewish and Christian readers see God's hidden care; critical readers note that the book leaves the question open on purpose.

sections.h: Persian law and the royal post (Esther 5–10)
sections.b: The second half of Esther shows the Persian court at work: the throne room at Susa (Esther 5:1), records of royal benefactors (Esther 6:1–3), confiscation of a traitor's estate (Esther 8:1), the king's signet ring as the power to make law (Esther 8:2, 8), a decree that cannot be revoked and so must be answered by another (Esther 8:8), letters sent in every script and language by the swift horses of the royal post (Esther 8:9–14), and tribute laid on land and islands (Esther 10:1). Greek writers such as Herodotus confirm many of these customs; no Persian text states the rule that a royal law cannot be revoked, though Diodorus (17.30) tells of a Persian king unable to undo his own order.

After the counter-decree, "many people from the peoples of the land made themselves Jews" (Esther 8:17). The rare verb may mean conversion (the Greek says they were circumcised), pretense, or taking the Jews' side. Purim is then made binding on the Jews, their descendants and "everyone who would join them" (Esther 9:27), the word Isaiah uses for foreigners who join themselves to the LORD (Isaiah 56:3–6).

Esther's letter places Purim beside "the fasts and their cries for help" that the Jews had taken on themselves (Esther 9:31), looking back to the fasting of Esther 4:3 and 4:16. The Fast of Esther, kept on the 13th of Adar, rests on this verse; it is not mentioned in the Talmud and first appears in the geonic She'iltot and the tractate Soferim. The Septuagint of Esther 9:31 has no fasts at all, and it lacks Esther 9:30. Zechariah's promise that fasts would become feasts (Zechariah 8:19) shares the pair "peace and truth" with Esther 9:30.

sections.h: A rescue far from the land (Esther 8–10)
sections.b: The rescue in Esther happens wholly in the diaspora. The counter-decree is sent "to the Jews in their own script and their own language" across 127 provinces (Esther 8:9), Purim is kept "province by province, city by city" (Esther 9:28), and the book ends not with a return to Zion but with a Jew second to the Persian king, working for his people (Esther 10:3). Esther's plea, "sold as slaves, men and women" (Esther 7:4), echoes the last exile curse of Deuteronomy 28:68. Many scholars read the book as a guide for Jewish life among the nations.

Haman builds a pole fifty cubits high for Mordecai (Esther 5:14) and is hanged on it himself (Esther 7:9–10). After his ten sons are killed, Esther asks that their bodies be hung on the pole for display (Esther 9:13–14), as Joshua hung the bodies of the five kings (Joshua 10:26) and as the Philistines hung Saul's (1 Samuel 31:10). The Greek of Esther 7:9 has the king order Haman "crucified."
sections.refs: Esther 5:14; Esther 7:9–10; Esther 9:13–14; Esther 9:25; Joshua 10:26; 1 Samuel 31:10; Deuteronomy 21:22–23

sections.b: Mordecai's letter recalls that Haman "had cast Pur, that is, the lot, to rout them in panic and destroy them" (Esther 9:24), and so "these days were named Purim, from the name Pur" (Esther 9:26). The Greek calls the festival Phrourai. In the Greek ending (Addition F), God makes two lots, one for his people and one for the nations, turning Haman's lot into God's.

sections.h: The plotter caught in his plot (Esther 7; 9:25)
sections.b: Haman is hanged on the pole he set up for Mordecai (Esther 7:10), and Mordecai's letter says his evil plot came back "on his own head" (Esther 9:25). The pattern matches the sayings that the one who digs a pit falls into it (Psalm 7:15–16; Proverbs 26:27) and Daniel's accusers thrown to the lions (Daniel 6:24). In Esther the reversal comes through human actions, with no named act of God.

Esther 9 uses the language of Israel's old wars ("dread of the Jews had come down on them," Esther 8:17; 9:2) but describes fighting under a Persian decree. Readers take it as lawful self-defense against an irrevocable decree (Baldwin, Bush, Berlin), as revenge (Paton; Luther disliked the book, though his stated complaint was that it and 2 Maccabees "Judaize too much"), or as a story of reversal written to give hope to a powerless people (Fox, Levenson). Unlike Saul, the Jews take no plunder (Esther 9:10, 15, 16).

sections.h: Gifts to the poor at Purim (Esther 9:22)
sections.b: Mordecai's letter makes "presents to the needy" part of the feast (Esther 9:22). Purim law requires gifts to at least two poor people (Bavli Megillah 7a), and Maimonides taught that it is better to give more to the poor than to make one's own feast more lavish (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Megillah 2:17).

Esther 9:32 ends with Esther's word "written in the book." The Talmud tells that Esther asked the sages to write her down for the generations (Bavli Megillah 7a), and records the view that the scroll does not "make the hands unclean." No copy of Esther has been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and Athanasius listed it among books to be read rather than the canon (Festal Letter 39).

Where the Hebrew is silent, the Greek speaks: "God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness" (Greek Esther 5:1e), "the Lord took the sleep away from the king" (Greek Esther 6:1), "the living God is with him" (Greek Esther 6:13), the king's letter calls the Jews children of "the Most High, the most mighty living God" (Addition E), and Mordecai ends, "These things have come from God" (Addition F). Jewish tradition found God's name hidden in letter patterns such as Esther 5:4 and 7:7, though most scholars think these are chance.
sections.refs: Esther 5:1–4; Esther 6:1; Esther 6:13; Esther 7:7; Esther 8:12; Esther 10:3

sections.b: Esther 7:7 uses the idiom of 1 Samuel 20:7 and 20:33 for a king who "had settled on" harm, and Esther 9:10–16 has the Jews refuse the plunder Saul took from Amalek (1 Samuel 15:9, 19). Mordecai, "the son of Kish, a man of Benjamin" (Esther 2:5), completes what Saul son of Kish left undone with Agag.
sections.refs: Esther 7:7; Esther 9:10–16; 1 Samuel 15:9; 1 Samuel 15:19; 1 Samuel 20:7; 1 Samuel 20:33

sections.b: Mordecai's honor follows Joseph's: royal clothes, a ride on the king's horse with a herald calling ahead (Esther 6:9–11; Genesis 41:42–43), the signet ring (Esther 8:2), and the place second to the king (Esther 10:3; Genesis 41:40). Haman "kept control of himself" with Joseph's verb (Esther 5:10; Genesis 43:31), and Esther's "How could I stand to watch" (Esther 8:6) echoes Judah's plea (Genesis 44:34).

sections.h: A feast not in the law of Moses (Esther 9)
sections.b: Purim is the one festival in the Hebrew Bible set up by Jewish leaders rather than commanded in the law of Moses. The Jews "set it up and took it on as binding" (Esther 9:27), a verse later Judaism used to show how binding customs could be added. Hanukkah, from the Maccabean period, followed the same pattern outside the Hebrew Bible.

sections.h: The Greek Additions to Esther (D, E, F)
sections.b: The Greek Esther adds six long passages. In the second half of the book: Addition D replaces Esther 5:1–2 with Esther's fainting before the king and God changing his heart; Addition E, after Esther 8:12, gives the king's second letter, calling Haman a Macedonian and the Jews children of the Most High; Addition F, after Esther 10:3, explains Mordecai's dream and adds a colophon saying the Greek "letter of Phrourai" was brought to Egypt "in the fourth year of Ptolemy and Cleopatra." Additions B and E were composed in Greek; A, C, D and F may go back to a Hebrew or Aramaic original (Moore). Catholic and Orthodox Christians read them as Scripture; Jews and Protestants do not.

Esther survives in two Greek forms: the Septuagint (B-text) and the shorter Alpha Text. In Esther 8–10 they differ most: the Septuagint lacks 9:5, has 15,000 dead in 9:16 instead of 75,000, and names the feast Phrourai (9:26); in 9:29–31 it has no "second" letter, lacks 9:30 and has no fasts; the Alpha Text tells the end in its own way, has Esther ask leave to destroy and plunder (9:13), and lacks most of 9:20–32. Clines argued the Alpha Text preserves an older story that ended at 8:17; others think it is a shortening.
